title: Birthmarks: Probably Not the Mark of the Devil
summary: Josh and Chuck explore birthmarks: their common types (vascular and pigmented), why they are reddish or brownish, and what causes them (science doesn't fully know). They cover flat vascular marks like angel kisses and stork bites, port wine stains and the link to Sturge-Webber syndrome and a GNAQ-type gene, strawberry hemangiomas, the blue-appearing deep hemangiomas, Mongolian spots, cafe au lait spots and neurofibromatosis type 1, and congenital, acquired and atypical moles with the melanoma risk. The hosts discuss social stigma and bullying, pulsed dye laser treatment for vascular marks, camouflage makeup, folk superstitions and pregnancy-cause myths, a past-life birthmark story, Russian nobility displaying birthmarks, and close with listener mail featuring band names. Ad reads and sponsor plugs (coffee thermos, rice cooker) appear mid-episode alongside tour dates and banter.

segments.title: Opening banter and birthmark chat
segments.summary: Hosts open with tour dates, then trade stories about their own skin tags, warts, freckles and birthmarks, and touch on stigma toward people with visible birthmarks.

segments.title: What birthmarks are and the main categories
segments.summary: Birthmarks are usually harmless and science does not fully know their cause. They are grouped into vascular (blood-vessel, usually reddish) and pigmented (melanin-based, usually brown) types.

segments.title: Flat vascular marks and port wine stains
segments.summary: Flat vascular marks such as angel kisses and stork bites often fade by age two to three. Port wine stains are different: they come from overdeveloped blood vessels, may darken and thicken over time, and are linked to a gene found while studying Sturge-Webber syndrome, which occurs in about six percent of cases.

segments.title: Strawberry hemangiomas and blue deep birthmarks
segments.summary: Strawberry hemangiomas are raised, reddish marks that appear in the first weeks of life and usually disappear by the early school years. Deeper ones can look bluish because less blue light penetrates, and rarely they involve internal organs.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break with a sponsor plug for a thermos and talk about rice cookers and sushi.

segments.title: Pigmented marks: cafe au lait spots and Mongolian spots
segments.summary: Pigmented marks are caused by clusters of melanin cells. Cafe au lait spots can signal neurofibromatosis type 1 if there are six or more, especially larger than a dime. Mongolian spots look like bruises, are bluish gray, usually on the lower back, and fade by about age six or seven.

segments.title: Moles: congenital, acquired and atypical
segments.summary: Moles are a type of pigmented birthmark. Congenital moles affect about one percent of babies and often have hair. Acquired moles appear later and may be linked to sun damage. Atypical moles are irregular in shape and color and are associated with melanoma, which the hosts stress is serious. They discuss beauty marks as celebrity features.

segments.title: Message break
segments.summary: Brief break before the treatment segment.

segments.title: Treatment and camouflage
segments.summary: Doctors usually monitor birthmarks rather than treat them. Vascular marks such as port wine stains and hemangiomas may respond to pulsed dye laser treatment, best started when the child is young. Pigmented marks are harder to treat. Camouflage makeup training is available, and facial differences and bullying are discussed.

segments.title: Birthmark superstitions and folklore
segments.summary: Folk beliefs include witchcraft, Satan's touch, and maternal causes such as startling or eating red foods. Chinese foot-location beliefs and Japanese fire myths are mentioned, along with a past-life birthmark story from Syria. Russian nobility displayed birthmarks as proof of status, and the hosts note genetic inheritance may explain some marks.

segments.title: Closing advice and listener mail band names
segments.summary: Hosts urge kids not to tease peers with birthmarks, then read listener mail from Ryan and Lucy, a list of band names submitted by listeners.
